Input nonnegative integers $m,n$ and coefficients $c_0,\ldots,c_{m+n}\in
\mathbb C$ of a formal power series or of an analytic function at $0$. Set
$c_k=0$ for negative $k$. Seek a normalized denominator
$q(z)=1+\sum_{j=1}^nq_jz^j$. Form the $n\times n$ moment system
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_jc_{m+\ell-j}=-c_{m+\ell}, \qquad 1\le\ell\le n.$$
Classify it by exact Gaussian elimination on the augmented matrix. Start with
pivot row $r=1$ and scan columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ in order. In column $j$, if
all entries in rows $r$ through $n$ are zero, leave that column free and
continue. Otherwise choose the first row $s\ge r$ with a nonzero entry in
column $j$, swap rows $s$ and $r$, divide row $r$ by its column-$j$ entry,
and subtract the resulting row multiple from every other row to make the
other entries in column $j$ zero; then increment $r$. After all columns, a
row whose coefficient entries are all zero and whose augmented entry is
nonzero makes the system inconsistent, so return status
$\texttt{full-order-inconsistent}$. If the system is consistent but has
rank less than $n$, return status $\texttt{defective-nonunique}$ together
with the rank and reduced system; do not select a denominator from its
affine solution set. Here rank is the number of pivot rows; consistency and rank are
read from the reduced augmented matrix. If the system has rank $n$, return status
$\texttt{full-order-solvable}$ and the unique solution
$(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$ and set
$$p_k=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}q_jc_{k-j}, \qquad 0\le k\le m,\qquad q_0:=1.$$
The output is the coefficient-matching candidate $p/q$ with its full-order
status. If $n=0$, return status $\texttt{full-order-solvable}$ with the empty
denominator system's unique solution $q=1$ and numerator coefficients
$p_k=c_k$ for $0\le k\le m$.
This procedure claims no pole-location or analytic-continuation guarantee.

For each $m<k\le m+n$, write $k=m+\ell$ with $1\le\ell\le n$. The moment equation in [F1] says $\sum_{j=1}^nq_jc_{k-j}=-c_k$, exactly the assertion that the degree-$k$ coefficient of $qf$ is zero, because $q_0=1$. Therefore every coefficient of $qf-p$ through degree $m+n$ vanishes.

Analyticity implies $qf-p$ has a Taylor expansion whose first possibly nonzero term has degree at least $m+n+1$, so $qf-p=O(z^{m+n+1})$. Let $q\ge 0$, let $t_0,\ldots,t_q$ be distinct real numbers, and let $f$ be
real-valued at these nodes. Define the **divided difference** recursively by
$f[t_0]:=f(t_0)$ and, for $q\ge1$,
$$f[t_0,\ldots,t_q]:= \frac{f[t_1,\ldots,t_q]-f[t_0,\ldots,t_{q-1}]}{t_q-t_0}.$$
All sublists in the recursion remain distinct. The denominator is nonzero
because $t_q\ne t_0$, so this recursion gives a finite real number from the
node data.

For distinct real nodes $t_0,\ldots,t_q$ and assigned values $f(t_j)$,
$$f[t_0,\ldots,t_q] =\sum_{j=0}^{q}\frac{f(t_j)}{\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le q\\k\ne j}}(t_j-t_k)}.$$
Consequently the divided difference is symmetric in its nodes. It is the
coefficient of $t^q$ in the unique polynomial of degree at most $q$ that takes
the assigned values at those nodes.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

In the recursive rule [F1], express the two order-$(q-1)$ divided differences by the induction hypothesis. The bottom face $u_q=0$ has argument $t_0+\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}u_j(t_j-t_0)$ and gives $f[t_0,\ldots,t_{q-1}]$. On the top face $u_q=1-\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}u_j$, the same argument is $t_q+\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}u_j(t_j-t_q)$ and gives $f[t_1,\ldots,t_q]$ by symmetry [F2]. The derivative is continuous by [F3], hence Riemann integrable. Applying [F4] on the $u_q$ interval, followed by integration over the other coordinates, shows that the difference of the two face integrals is $(t_q-t_0)$ times the $q$-dimensional integral in the statement. When the outer coordinates sum to $1$, the inner $u_q$ interval is $[0,0]$ and its integral is zero; for $q=1$ there are no outer coordinates and the interval is $[0,1]$. Division by $t_q-t_0\ne0$ gives the order-$q$ formula.

By [F6], prove the volume formula by induction, with its $q=0$ case from step 1.1. For $q\ge1$, fix the outer coordinate $u_1\in[0,1]$. The remaining coordinates form a $(q-1)$-simplex scaled by $1-u_1$. If $q=1$, its zero-dimensional volume is $1$; if $q\ge2$ and $u_1<1$, the dilation to $\Delta_{q-1}$ has Jacobian $(1-u_1)^{q-1}$, while the section at $u_1=1$ has $(q-1)$-volume zero. Thus, by induction, the section volume is $(1-u_1)^{q-1}/(q-1)!$. The function $H(u)=-(1-u)^q/q!$ has derivative $(1-u)^{q-1}/(q-1)!$; applying [F4] to $H$ on $[0,1]$ gives $H(1)-H(0)=1/q!$. $$\operatorname{vol}(\Delta_q) =\int_0^1\frac{(1-u_1)^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}\,du_1 =\frac1{q!}.$$ The induction and the divided-difference identity prove the statement.

Input a nonempty ordered list of distinct sample points
$Z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\subset\mathbb C$, data
$F=(f_1,\ldots,f_N)\in\mathbb C^N$, an absolute tolerance $\tau\ge0$, an
integer support budget $B$ with $0\le B\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor$, and a finite integer
bidiagonal-QR sweep budget $S\ge0$. The procedure is evaluated in exact
arithmetic; its finite-precision implementation makes no optimality claim.
For $v\in\mathbb C^k$, use the standard Hermitian inner product and Euclidean
norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^k|v_j|^2)^{1/2}$.
Initialize the accepted support-record list $S_{\rm acc}=\varnothing$; each
record stores an original index, its sample point, and its data value. Set the
remaining original-index list $R=(1,\ldots,N)$. Every return has form
$(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\text{status},\mathcal R)$, where $\mathcal R$ is
the residual record maintained below.

1. Set the initial rational candidate $r_0$ to the constant mean
$\bar f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$. Compute
$\eta_0=\max_i|f_i-\bar f|$, set the last accepted candidate $r_{\rm acc}=r_0$,
and set $\mathcal R=((0,\eta_0))$. If $\eta_0\le\tau$, return
$(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{tolerance-met},\mathcal R)$.

2. For $m=1,\ldots,B$, choose from $R$ the least original index $s$ that
maximizes the absolute residual from $r_{\rm acc}$. Let $S_{\rm prov}$ be
$S_{\rm acc}$ with $(s,z_s,f_s)$ appended; remove $s$ from $R$.

3. Form the $(N-m)\times m$ Loewner matrix
$L_{ij}=(f_i-f_{s_j})/(z_i-z_{s_j})$, where $i$ ranges over the indices in
$R$ and $s_j$ are the original indices in $S_{\rm prov}$. The denominator is
nonzero because all sample points are distinct.

4. Compute an exact full singular value decomposition (SVD) of $L$ by applying
[[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] followed by
[[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]] with zero deflation
tolerance and budget $S$. If either call returns failure or the QR budget is
exhausted, return $(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{inconclusive},\mathcal R)$.

5. Let $E$ be the right singular subspace for the smallest singular value of
$L$, and let $P_E$ be its orthogonal projection. Choose the least coordinate
index $j$ for which $P_Ee_j\ne0$ and set $w=P_Ee_j/\|P_Ee_j\|_2$. This rule
applies at every multiplicity, including dimension one. Multiply by the
unique unit scalar that makes the first nonzero coordinate of $w$ positive
real. If any coordinate of $w$ is zero, reject this provisional support and
return $(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{zero-support-weight},\mathcal R)$.

6. Form the barycentric rational quotient using the nodes and data in
$S_{\rm prov}$ and $w$ as its weights. If this rational function has a
genuine pole at any remaining sample point, reject this provisional support
and return $(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{pole-status},\mathcal R)$.
Otherwise accept the candidate by setting $r_{\rm acc}$ to it and
$S_{\rm acc}=S_{\rm prov}$, and append $(m,\eta_m,\sigma_m)$, where $\eta_m$
is its maximum sampled residual and $\sigma_m=\|Lw\|_2$, to $\mathcal R$. If
$\eta_m\le\tau$, return
$(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{tolerance-met},\mathcal R)$.

7. If all $B$ iterations finish without another return, return
$(r_{\rm acc},S_{\rm acc},\texttt{support-budget-exhausted},\mathcal R)$. In
particular $B=0$ returns the initial constant and empty support list with this
status when step 1 does not return.

The support tie rule and the projection rule make the exact procedure
deterministic, including when the smallest singular value has multiplicity
greater than one. Rank deficiency is permitted: if the smallest singular
value is zero and all selected weights are nonzero and the quotient is finite
at the remaining sample points, the candidate is accepted and its exact
sample residual is evaluated. The algorithm asserts no uniform off-grid error
bound and no minimax optimality. The Loewner residual $\sigma_m$ is a linear
least-squares residual, not the nonlinear sampled residual $\eta_m$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For the data and nonzero weights in [[def-barycentric-rational-quotient]],
$Q$ is not the zero polynomial, the rational function $P/Q$ is well-defined,
and $r(z_j)=f_j$ for each support node $z_j$.

derivations.claim: Let $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ be a full orthonormal right singular-vector basis for $L$, with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_m\ge0$ and $\sigma_m=\sigma_{\min}(L)$. For any unit vector $v=\sum_jc_jv_j$, orthonormality gives $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, and the SVD gives $$\|Lv\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sigma_j^2|c_j|^2 \ge\sigma_m^2.$$ The selected $w$ lies in the right singular subspace for $\sigma_m$, so equality holds. Hence $\|Lw\|_2=\sigma_{\min}(L)$ and no unit vector gives a smaller Loewner residual.

The right singular subspace $E$ is nonzero. If every projection $P_Ee_j$ of a coordinate basis vector vanished, then every vector of $E$ would be orthogonal to every coordinate basis vector and hence would be zero, a contradiction. Thus the least index with nonzero projection exists; the normalization and phase convention in [F1] choose a unique unit vector in $E$, also when the smallest singular value is repeated or zero.

On the successful-weight branch, every support weight is nonzero. By [F3], the barycentric quotient is defined and its value at each selected support node is the corresponding datum. The candidate is returned only after the algorithm's reduced-denominator pole check succeeds at all remaining sample points, so its finite residual there is defined.

Each iteration removes one previously remaining point and the budget satisfies $B\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor$. Every branch either returns immediately or proceeds to the next integer $m\le B$, so the algorithm makes at most $B$ iterations and terminates. The minimized quantity in step 1.1 is $\|Lw\|_2$; the procedure separately records $\eta_m$ and makes no minimax or uniform-error claim.

$f_0,\ldots,f_n\in\mathbb R$ be data, and let $d$ be an integer with
$0\le d<n$. For $j=0,\ldots,n$, define
$$w_j=(-1)^{j-d} \sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)} \prod_{\substack{i\le k\le i+d\\k\ne j}}|x_j-x_k|^{-1}.$$
The index range is nonempty and every product is positive, so every $w_j$ is
nonzero. The **Floater–Hormann interpolant of degree parameter $d$** is the
barycentric rational quotient of these nodes, data, and weights from
[[def-barycentric-rational-quotient]]. Away from the nodes, exact evaluation
uses the quotient with this denominator;
a zero of the reduced denominator is reported as pole status. The no-real-pole
theorem below proves that this status never occurs for admissible exact real
inputs.

For the nodes, data, and degree parameter of
[[def-floater-hormann-interpolant]], let $0\le i\le n-d$. The local
**window polynomial** is
$$p_i(t)=\sum_{k=i}^{i+d}f_k \prod_{\substack{i\le j\le i+d\\j\ne k}} \frac{t-x_j}{x_k-x_j}.$$
All denominators are nonzero because the nodes are distinct. Empty products
equal one, in particular when $d=0$.

For each window $i$, the polynomial $p_i$ in
[[def-floater-hormann-window-polynomial]] has degree at most $d$ and satisfies
$p_i(x_k)=f_k$ for every $i\le k\le i+d$. It is the unique polynomial of
degree at most $d$ with those values. In particular, when all local data
equal $1$, the local Lagrange basis functions sum to the constant polynomial
$1$.

Let $k\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_k\in\mathbb C$ be distinct support nodes, let
$f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathbb C$ be data, and let each weight $w_j\in\mathbb C$ be
nonzero. Define the cleared polynomials
$$P(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_jf_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell), \qquad Q(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell).$$
The **barycentric rational quotient** is the rational function $r=P/Q$.
Away from the support nodes this equals
$$r(z)= \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_jf_j/(z-z_j)} {\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_j/(z-z_j)}.$$
At a support node its value is given by the cleared quotient $P(z_j)/Q(z_j)$.
A **pole** means a zero of the denominator after all common polynomial
factors of numerator and denominator have been canceled.

derivations.claim: Put $P_0(x)=\prod_{j=0}^n(x-x_j)$ and $m=n-d$. Counting the $m$ factors to the right of a window gives $$\mu_i(x)=(-1)^mP_0(x)\lambda_i(x).$$ Indeed, after cancellation each right factor $x_k-x$ contributes one minus sign when rewritten as $x-x_k$, and the remaining denominator factors are exactly the window nodes. Thus the cleared products agree as polynomials, including at nodes; summing gives the stated cleared-denominator identity. Away from nodes it also shows that the blend quotient with $\lambda_i$ equals the quotient with $\mu_i$ and $s$.

Expand each $p_i$ using [F2], and interchange the two finite sums. The coefficient of $f_j/(x-x_j)$ in $\sum_i\lambda_i p_i$ is $$\widetilde w_j= \sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)} (-1)^i\prod_{\substack{i\le k\le i+d\\k\ne j}} \frac1{x_j-x_k}.$$ Within a window exactly $i+d-j$ factors $x_j-x_k$ are negative, so each summand has sign $(-1)^{2i+d-j}=(-1)^{j-d}$ and absolute value $\prod_{k\ne j}|x_j-x_k|^{-1}$. Thus $\widetilde w_j=w_j$ as in [F1].

The same expansion for constant data $f_k=1$ has each window polynomial equal to $1$ by [F2]. Therefore the coefficient of $1/(x-x_j)$ in $\sum_i\lambda_i$ is also $\widetilde w_j=w_j$. Dividing the expanded numerator by the expanded denominator proves that the blend equals the barycentric quotient in [F3] away from support nodes.

At a node $x_\alpha$, $\mu_i(x_\alpha)$ is zero unless $\max(0,\alpha-d)\le i\le\min(\alpha,m)$; for these indices all its factors are positive. This index set is nonempty, and every corresponding window contains $x_\alpha$. By [F2], $p_i(x_\alpha)=f_\alpha$, so the blend has numerator $f_\alpha s(x_\alpha)$ and $s(x_\alpha)>0$. Its value is therefore $f_\alpha$, agreeing with the support convention in [F3].

Input nonnegative integers $m,n$ and coefficients $c_0,\ldots,c_{m+n}\in
\mathbb C$ of a formal power series or of an analytic function at $0$. Set
$c_k=0$ for negative $k$. Seek a normalized denominator
$q(z)=1+\sum_{j=1}^nq_jz^j$. Form the $n\times n$ moment system
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_jc_{m+\ell-j}=-c_{m+\ell}, \qquad 1\le\ell\le n.$$
Classify it by exact Gaussian elimination on the augmented matrix. Start with
pivot row $r=1$ and scan columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ in order. In column $j$, if
all entries in rows $r$ through $n$ are zero, leave that column free and
continue. Otherwise choose the first row $s\ge r$ with a nonzero entry in
column $j$, swap rows $s$ and $r$, divide row $r$ by its column-$j$ entry,
and subtract the resulting row multiple from every other row to make the
other entries in column $j$ zero; then increment $r$. After all columns, a
row whose coefficient entries are all zero and whose augmented entry is
nonzero makes the system inconsistent, so return status
$\texttt{full-order-inconsistent}$. If the system is consistent but has
rank less than $n$, return status $\texttt{defective-nonunique}$ together
with the rank and reduced system; do not select a denominator from its
affine solution set. Here rank is the number of pivot rows; consistency and rank are
read from the reduced augmented matrix. If the system has rank $n$, return status
$\texttt{full-order-solvable}$ and the unique solution
$(q_1,\ldots,q_n)$ and set
$$p_k=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}q_jc_{k-j}, \qquad 0\le k\le m,\qquad q_0:=1.$$
The output is the coefficient-matching candidate $p/q$ with its full-order

Let $n\ge1$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, let
$f_0,\ldots,f_n\in\mathbb R$ be data, and let $d$ be an integer with
$0\le d<n$. For $j=0,\ldots,n$, define
$$w_j=(-1)^{j-d} \sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)} \prod_{\substack{i\le k\le i+d\\k\ne j}}|x_j-x_k|^{-1}.$$
The index range is nonempty and every product is positive, so every $w_j$ is
nonzero. The **Floater–Hormann interpolant of degree parameter $d$** is the
barycentric rational quotient of these nodes, data, and weights from
[[def-barycentric-rational-quotient]]. Away from the nodes, exact evaluation
uses the quotient with this denominator;
a zero of the reduced denominator is reported as pole status. The no-real-pole
theorem below proves that this status never occurs for admissible exact real
inputs.

For any $n\ge1$, any distinct ordered real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, any real
data $f_0,\ldots,f_n$, and any integer $0\le d<n$, the exact
Floater–Hormann rational function in
[[def-floater-hormann-interpolant]] has no real poles.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $k\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_k\in\mathbb C$ be distinct support nodes, let
$f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathbb C$ be data, and let each weight $w_j\in\mathbb C$ be
nonzero. Define the cleared polynomials
$$P(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_jf_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell), \qquad Q(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}(z-z_\ell).$$
The **barycentric rational quotient** is the rational function $r=P/Q$.
Away from the support nodes this equals
$$r(z)= \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_jf_j/(z-z_j)} {\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_j/(z-z_j)}.$$
At a support node its value is given by the cleared quotient $P(z_j)/Q(z_j)$.
A **pole** means a zero of the denominator after all common polynomial
factors of numerator and denominator have been canceled.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

derivations.claim: Fix $d\ge0$. For every integer $n\ge2d+2$, take $h=1/n$, $x_j=jh$ on $[0,1]$, and query $x=h/2$. This family has $h/h_{\min}=1$. From [F1], after multiplying every weight by the same positive factor $h^dd!$, its weights are $$\widetilde w_j=(-1)^{j-d}\delta_j,\qquad \delta_j=\sum_{i=\max(0,j-d)}^{\min(j,n-d)}\binom d{j-i}.$$ Indeed, on a uniform mesh each reciprocal-distance product in [F1] equals $h^{-d}/((j-i)!(i+d-j)!)$. Thus $1\le\delta_j\le2^d$, and $\delta_j=2^d$ for $d\le j\le n-d$.

Define $$\phi(t)= \begin{cases} (1-16t^2)^{d+2},& |t|\le1/4,\\ 0,& |t|>1/4. \end{cases}$$ At both support endpoints the polynomial has a zero of multiplicity $d+2$, so its derivatives through order $d+1$ vanish there and agree with the zero extension; hence $\phi\in C^{d+1}(\mathbb R)$ and $\phi(0)=1$. Expanding the polynomial and differentiating each term gives $$\|\phi^{(d+1)}\|_\infty\le M_d:=4^{d+1} \sum_{k=\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil}^{d+2} \binom{d+2}{k}\frac{(2k)!}{(2k-d-1)!}<\infty.$$ This is a finite bound depending only on $d$, and its $k=d+2$ term shows $M_d>0$.

Let $D(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\widetilde w_j/(x-x_j)$ be the denominator at the query. If $d=0$, its $j=0$ term has magnitude $2/h$, and the remaining terms form an alternating decreasing sequence beginning with magnitude $2/h$, so $|D(x)|\le4/h$. If $d\ge1$, the endpoint blocks $j=0,\ldots,d-1$ and $j=n-d+1,\ldots,n$ each contain $d$ terms of magnitude at most $2^{d+1}/h$. The middle block $j=d,\ldots,n-d$ has constant $\delta_j=2^d$ and alternating decreasing magnitudes, so its sum has magnitude at most $2^{d+1}/h$. Hence in both cases $$0<|D(x)|\le \frac{2^d(4d+4)}h,$$ The strict lower inequality follows from [F2].

The real number $\widetilde w_j/(x-x_j)$ is nonzero. Define $\sigma_j=1$ if it is positive and $\sigma_j=-1$ if it is negative, and set $$f_n(t)=h^{d+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n} \sigma_j\phi\!\left(\frac{t-x_j}{h}\right),\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$ The supports have radius $h/4$ about distinct nodes, so they are disjoint; the query $x=h/2$ is outside every support. Therefore $f_n(x)=0$, $f_n(x_j)=h^{d+1}\sigma_j$, $f_n\in C^{d+1}([0,1])$, and $\|f_n^{(d+1)}\|_\infty\le M_d$ by [F3] and the derivative estimate in step 1.2.

By the barycentric quotient formula [F4] and the signs $\sigma_j$, the numerator at $x$ is $h^{d+1}\sum_j|\widetilde w_j/(x-x_j)|$. Restricting to $j=d+1,\ldots,n-d$ and using $\delta_j=2^d$ and $|x-x_j|=h(j-\tfrac12)$, step 2.1 gives $$|f_n(x)-r_d(x)| \ge\frac{h^{d+1}}{4d+4} \sum_{j=d+1}^{n-d}\frac1{j-\tfrac12}.$$ Since $t\mapsto1/(t-\tfrac12)$ is decreasing, $$\sum_{j=d+1}^{n-d}\frac1{j-\tfrac12} \ge \int_{d+1}^{n-d+1}\frac{dt}{t-\tfrac12} =\log\frac{n-d+\tfrac12}{d+\tfrac12}.$$ This lower bound grows without limit as $n$ increases.

By [F2], $f_n-r_d$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, so [F5] makes its uniform norm finite. It follows that $$\frac{\|f_n-r_d\|_\infty} {h^{d+1}M_d} \ge \frac{\log((n-d+\tfrac12)/(d+\tfrac12))} {(4d+4)M_d} \longrightarrow\infty \qquad(n\to\infty).$$ Every mesh in the family has ratio one, but no fixed $C(d,1)$ can satisfy the refuted inequality. Thus it fails even at $\rho=1$ for each fixed $d$.
